en: Bow down to the evening water-offering of the cowherd, which holds a lotus as its oblation, and in which the moon— the face of Gaurī— reflected in his red-with-anger countenance appears like a bee.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 1) Those who do not know how to read or hear the nectar-like poetry of Pāyaka...

They perform the piercing of the heart of desire; how are they not ashamed? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 2) Seven hundred [verses], along with a million [others], composed by Hāla in the midst of his poetic skill, consist of stanzas adorned with poetic figures. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 3)
Motionless and still, the female crane shines upon the lotus leaf like a conch-shell necklace resting in a vessel of pure emerald. Thus,
at the time of twilight, the graceful charms of women shine forth.
Until her eyes, with their luster like blue water-lily petals, close in sleep.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 5) O Kuravaka tree, why do you not seek for yourself that which you desire?
O fortunate one, it is your own wife who smiles thus at you with her face turned. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 6)
In the absence of their lovers, those charming young women are tormented by sorrows;
for who, even when powerful, can endure the kick of anyone's foot? O mother, so delightful is our village, having become its very ornament... [Gāthāsaptaśatī 7]...
[Attā 1]... so delightful is our village, having become its very ornament.
The lotus thicket, its stalks bent low by the frost, resembles a skull-bowl (kapāla).
Why do you weep with downcast face amidst the white rice fields?
O girl, your face adorned with green [mud] has become like a hemp-field.

My friend, such indeed is the course of love; do not weep for it, which is as crooked as a thread pulled by a child—its face wrinkled with frowns. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 10) When the son climbed onto the back of his father who had fallen at his feet...

The husband departed from his home, leaving behind his wife who was deeply tormented by her intense grief. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 11) "Know that he speaks the truth; such behavior is appropriate toward a person like him.
Let him die, but I will not say anything to you; even death would be praiseworthy for him. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 12)

"O you skilled in the work of cooking, do not be distressed; the fire smokes as it inhales the fragrant breath from her mouth, which is like a red *pāṭala* flower, but it does not blaze up, because her hand—stained with soot from the kitchen work—is still upon it. (Gāthāsaṃgraha 13)
Her heart was smiling broadly as her husband looked upon her face, which had taken on the appearance of the moon.
When asked by her friends, "What, what does it look like? the innocent girl, longing for the first flush of pregnancy, simply directed her gaze toward her lover. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 14–15)

O Moon, crest-jewel of the sky and tilaka-mark on the face of night, touch me with those very same rays by which you have conquered my heart; let him who has gone abroad come here, and if he should become angry, let him appease me. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 16) Let him indeed come, and if he should be offended, let him also be conciliated.
This garland of lovely flowers bears fruit for someone; it falls upon my beloved. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 17) O friends, look!
How can I endure this tattered rag, washed with the tears trickling from my eyes, as it falls like a tear itself? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 18)

O you with ears as pale as the interior of a young lotus bud, as you go home with your heart fixed upon me, you shall attain whiteness [of fame]! O happy one, even though feigning sleep with eyes closed, grant me an opportunity! (Gāthāsaptaśatī 19)

"O you whose limbs are covered in wounds from the bite of the *gaṇḍa* plant, I shall not delay you again. (Gāthāsaṃgraha 20) Go home while your ornaments are still incomplete, my daughter; once you have been announced to him who is full of curiosity and has raised a great clamor, you will no longer remain in his heart. (Gāthāsaṃgraha 21)
We shall bear the embrace of her whose lips were bent in salutation, whose nose was not yet formed, whose forehead was ununited,
and whose face was smeared with the mixture of pigments— when,
during love-play, she gave him kisses upon his nose, her cheeks blossoming with joy. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 22)
Even at dawn, she remains with her face cast down; we cannot believe that this is for his sake.

Obeisance to that astrological birth-chart which causes you, O living being, to suffer both the pain of separation from a beloved and the sight of one who is not dear—both of which are grievous miseries. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 23–24)
Even a single black antelope, as it wanders clockwise, does not allow one to pass;
how much less so the pair of eyes of my beloved, which are filled with longing?
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 25) Not even practicing pride during the nights when they have awakened slightly from a pleasant sleep...
If you are aware of the pain of being robbed by one who has emptied his side [of the bed],
who then is the victor between two lovers who are both jealous, feigning sleep with false pretenses, while their sighs are held motionless and suppressed? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 26–27)

Wherever my beloved desires to strike a fresh blow upon my body, there a row of horripilation appears on the bride. Today, as I remember the pleasures experienced with him, [I am overcome].* *Note: The final line of the verse is incomplete in the source text; it is supplied here based on the standard structure of this verse in the *Gāthāsaptaśatī*. The sentiment is one of longing and the physical manifestation of that longing through horripilation.*
The sound of fresh clouds was heard, like a thunderbolt falling.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 29) O pitiless one, O you who fear your wife, O you of evil appearance, O you who resemble a dung-beetle!
Even so, the village has been wasted for your sake, O son of the village headman. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 30)
On the rough paths of the forest, she finds sleep only with great difficulty; yet in the chest of the village headman, that same village woman sleeps happily.
O fortunate one, it is you alone who have traversed the path that was truly worthy of being undertaken.
Nowadays, one thing is in the heart of the world and another is on their lips.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 32) Why, sighing hot breaths, do you burn my back with your resentment while lying on half the bed with your face turned away from me? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 33)

In her separation from you, O long-suffering one, the shadow has not even reached her face, which is stained by falling tears and appears as if struck by the peak of the mountain of passion. [Gāthāsaptaśatī 34] On the wall of the noble lady’s house, drawn by the unchaste mind of her brother-in-law...

Every day he recounts the adventures of Lakṣmaṇa, who followed Rāma. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 35) The wife of a traveler, the woman with a pleasing appearance, the young woman whose husband is away, the unchaste woman, and the woman difficult to approach through her companions—none of these have ever broken their virtue even for a moment. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 36)
With its filaments broken by the impact of the *tālūra* fish and its bees half-submerged and emerging as it is partially submerged by the flood of the mountain river,
the *kalamva* flower mocks the shadow of its husband, the inaccessible mountain, which is full of excessive pride.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 37) Protect the shadow of your husband!
The housewife grieves for her own kinsmen as they arrive with their wealth;

though her beloved is at hand and the festival has arrived, she does not adorn herself, as she is occupied with maintaining the savings earned through her husband’s hardships abroad. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 38–39)
Her heart is yours; her eyes have seen you;
her limbs, though withered by separation from you, are dear to her—even these things are beloved because they are filled with sincerity and overflowing with affection.
It is only right that one should be enamored of such devotion.
But when one gives with no heart at all, people laugh at that heart.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 41) For a man who undertakes an enterprise, prosperity is certain, or else death occurs;
that death may indeed come even without undertaking an enterprise, yet prosperity will not come. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 42)
The fire of separation from a beloved person can be endured through the bond of hope;
however, O Mother, living in the same village [without union] makes death itself seem more distinguished.
My beloved stirs within my heart as I take pleasure with other women.
When qualities similar to what has been seen are being surpassed by even more similar qualities;
when youth resembles a river in flood and the days have passed far away, and the nights do not return—my daughter, what is gained by burning with grief? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 44–45)
"It is said that it is well indeed when a husband returns from travel; so it is heard among the people.
Therefore, O noble sir, act in such a way that for this woman there is no 'tomorrow' at all.
[This is] the secret for sustaining life through the inquiry of a wife whose husband is about to depart on a journey.
She wanders from house to house asking [for news], unable to endure the separation from her beloved. "O Fate, grant our husband attachment to another woman!
Men who are exclusively devoted to passion do not indeed distinguish between faults and virtues. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 47–48)
Even though she does not go out even at dawn, look—she is lying on her back in the midday heat;
yet, out of fear of the sun, even the shade has fled. O traveler, why do you not rest?
[For] you are bringing to us from afar a person of lovely appearance, though difficult to find. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 49)
"O Ujjayinī, even if my life were departing, you would not be guilty of any offense.
"Yes, O Fever, I am dull-witted; or rather, what concern is it of people whether I am dull-witted or not?
O seeker of pleasure, O pleasant one, O sweet-smelling one, do not touch the Gandharī! (Gāthāsaptaśatī 50–51)

Know that the suffering of men is like a woman who, with her hair disheveled by the scratching of her fingernails and her eyes half-closed, gazes at a man with a sidelong glance— she who is the visible proof of the breach of the bond of love. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 52)

Even water, when heated and cooled, becomes tasteless. (Gāthāśataka 53) Upon hearing the sound of her husband’s loincloth, which was louder than the crash of a thunderbolt, even the eyes of the female cranes were filled with tears. (Gāthāśataka 54)
O Karimari, why do you vainly experience horripilation, longing for the sound of your husband’s bow, when this is merely the echo of the clouds thundering as they fall upon the mountain?
She was so enjoyed by that lover, who is skilled in the arts of love, that she endures it, yes, she endures it!

Her limbs have become like the beauty of a mountain peak. (Gāthāśataka 56) O youth, disregarding all other young men and having transcended worldly decorum, she wanders with her eyes cast toward the quarters of the sky for your sake. (Gāthāśataka 57)
This very day the festival of the night-watch has departed for people;
this very day the landing-stairs on the banks of the Godāvarī are once more yellowed by turmeric.
While the son-in-law is of an incompatible mind, the beloved is pure-hearted, yet fickle in disposition. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 58)
Out of fear that her family would be broken up, the daughter-in-law does not speak, though she has grown thin;
when the lover, delayed by anxiety, arrives, she, filled with feigned anger, quarrels until she makes him silent, and though her friends weep, they are not laughed at. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 59–60)
Just as tasks accomplished with those of equal status bring joy to the mind even when unfinished, they do not do so in the same way when performed by others, even if fully completed.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 61) [With its tail-tip smeared with the halāhala poison hidden within the slightly opened folds of its skin...]
Behold the tender mango sprout emerging from the stem! (GāSa.

62) Behold the young monkey, clinging to its own thread that has slipped through a hole in its skin and become entangled in its foot—like a single, knotted flower whose string is difficult to discern! (GāSa. 63)
The temple shrieks out its agony at being pierced by stakes, as the pigeons hidden in the crevices of the crumbling walls coo discordantly; it is like a deity struck by spears.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 64) If you are not his beloved, [you will suffer] day after day with limbs rendered helpless.
Why do you sleep as if intoxicated by the fresh scent of the wine of sleep? (GāSa.
65) During these winter nights that are so exceedingly long, you remain sleepless;
O wife whose husband has been away for a long time, it is not right that you should sleep during the day. (GāSa. 66)

O handsome one, if you have given me this foot of yours, which is weary from sinking into the mire, then why do you now bear a body that is being pricked by thorns? The festival has arrived, yet it does not shine for you, like the moon on the full-moon night when the sun is at its peak brilliance.
Love is like a poison that ends in bitterness, and joy is short-lived when it is not fulfilled.

(Gāthāsaptaśatī 68) Her good fortune was clearly recognized by her friends at the very moment of the marriage ceremony, once the serpent-bracelet had been cast far away by the lord of beasts. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 69)
In summer, the peaks of the Vindhya mountains appear as if covered with the soot of forest fires;
do not hope for fresh clouds in the rainy season for the wife who has gone abroad.
Give only as much of your favor as can be easily borne.
Not every person is capable of enduring the suffering that arises from the loss of favor.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 71) How could she who has been the beloved of a man with many favorites for five days seek a sixth? Where is there both sweetness and abundance? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 72)
Whichever part of my body he gazes upon with unblinking eyes, that very part I conceal;
yet I desire to be seen by him.
Behold, though she is deeply tormented by passion, she has been captured by her lover.
The pride of the gods and demons subsides like a handful of sand.
Behold, the row of parrots, entwined with rubies,
descends from the sky like a necklace slipped from the neck of the Goddess of Heaven.

Even so, the departure of all my attendants does not produce such grief or distress for me as the retreating circle of supplicants who have turned away from their desired object. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 76) A traveler was protected by the grass in the village against the forest fire, whereas in the forest he was consumed by it.
The city-dweller is tormented by the cold as if by resentment.

(Gāthā Saptaśatī 77) We shall drink her face, with its wide, trembling eyes and lips stained by the wine from her mouth, like a lotus covered by a swarm of bees agitated by its fragrance. (Gāthā Saptaśatī 78)
On the day of the festival, the good fortune of the co-wives—who had been purified by bathing with *hallaphala*—was, as it were, proclaimed by the noble lady through her command for them to bathe;
[and so too was it proclaimed] by the lattice-work of the window whose interior was filled with the turmeric paste from their bath. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 79)
They clean away stains with a blade of *kiliñca* grass; what purpose will you achieve by this? (GāSa.
80) Love perishes through non-seeing; it perishes even through excessive seeing;
it perishes through being moved by malicious people; it perishes even in this very way [through constant presence]. (GāSa. 81)

Suffering is endured by the sight of women, by the excessive sight of the low-born, and by the malicious and ignoble speech of the fool; likewise, it is endured by the wicked through their belly-aches after having been prosperous. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 82)
As she was thinking thus in her mind, the face of her breasts turned dark.
(Gāthāśataka 83) O beautiful one, that noble husband, the farmer, has wasted away so much for your sake that even his jealous wife has begun to accept a second [wife]. (Gāthāśataka 84)
O handsome one, coming with courtesy you gladden our hearts; what peace can there be for those from whom you have departed with such lack of affection?
Blowing upon my hand with the wind of your mouth, you struck it once with a blow.

He too was seized by me, laughing, by the neck with my hand. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 86) O proud woman, the thrill of horripilation on the back of your lover as he approaches you—who are turning your face away while being supported [by him]—tells that your heart is actually turned toward him. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 87)
Knowing [the situation] and wishing to make it known, she herself, even in private,
maintains her reliance on courtesy toward him whose pride has been crushed by her entreaties;
O Kṛṣṇa, as Rādhikā wipes away that pale mark with the breath from her mouth—
O fair one, you steal away the luster of these cowherd women and others as well.

O shameless one, tell me, have you committed such offenses against beautiful men in the past, are you doing so now, or will you do so in the future? Are those who commit them ever forgiven? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 89–90)
Those who bow before their superior and appease their anger like servants—they alone are the beloveds of women; the rest are merely wretched masters.
O bee, at that time you did not delight in other species of flowers.
O friend, you now abandon the jasmine creeper, heavy with its burden of ripened fruit;
yet, O mother, that very thirst has not been quenched by that sight—which was so wonderful to behold—that it was like a dream, or rather, like water seen in a mirage. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 92–93)
A traveler adorns the very place where he stays;

however, one who has uprooted a village and dwells nearby is like a great banyan tree that has been torn from its place. Only he is remembered who, though driven away, remains for even a moment in the hearts [of others].
The love that was to be cultivated has been accomplished, yet it remains without support.
Today, as if guarding her own destruction, that poor girl protects the circle of your teeth upon her cheek with a veil of rising horripilation. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 95–96)
The mango blossoms have been seen, the wine has been smelled, and the southern breeze has been enjoyed;
O friend, even such heavy tasks are accomplished—whom does love belong to?
When he returned from his pursuit, having gone only a single step after making love...
"Ah! At that very moment, he became like a woman whose husband has gone abroad, or like a traveler who has returned from afar. (GāSa.

98) "Through merits, a person finds another person who is a sight to be beheld without weariness, who shares equally in joy and sorrow, who has bestowed true affection, and whose heart is bound to one's own. (GāSa. 99)
Even one who causes pain produces happiness for whomsoever he becomes dear;
even for breasts scorched by the nails of the lover, the thrill of horripilation increases.
Though held and held, the advice given by dear friends falls apart.
In her heart, shattered by the blow of the god of love’s arrow...

(Gāthāsaptaśatī 101) With her mind solely intent on protecting the young *pīlu* tree standing on the riverbank, disregarding the danger of the downpour, a woman carries [the tree] along with the flood. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 102)
O Sahakāra tree, whose branches are bent down by the weight of many flowers; O Mahua tree of the dense thickets on the banks of the Godāvarī, hear my request: you must shed your blossoms slowly.
These last flowers of an unchaste woman are difficult for her to behold.
Like a woman weeping over the bones of her kinsman, she gathers them up.
O heart, like a long log being dragged through the waters of a narrow stream,
you will burn at every single spot where you get stuck.

That very redness of the beloved’s lips, which was kissed by him at night, is seen this morning reflected in the eyes of his co-wives. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 106) Having seen the son of the householder standing on the bank of the Godāvarī, the daughter-in-law of the farmer...

We have undertaken to cross over the path of suffering which is so difficult to traverse. (GāSa. 107) As he sits upon the footstool, though he speaks not, we shall experience the pleasure of firmly grasping his hair and twisting it around his big toe. (GāSa. 108)
Look! Like an axe, it splits the smoldering straw fire at the door of the temple in this wretched village, kindled by the cold of winter.
The lotus ponds have not been trampled, nor have the swans been startled, O aunt.

Someone has thrown a cloud over the village pond. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 110) By whom, with a heart whose desires were shattered, was it said "he is away on a journey," by which the limbs of the bride are languid as if filled with sorrow? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 111)
"Even now Dāmaoara is a child," having been told this by Yaśodā,
the young wives laughed silently, their eyes fixed upon the face of Kṛṣṇa.
Those few are truly virtuous men whose affection does not depend on the expression of the face.

Increasing day by day, it passes on to his sons like a debt. (Gāthā Saptaśatī 113) Under the pretext of praising his dancing, a clever cowherd woman standing nearby kisses Kṛṣṇa as he appears in the reflection upon the cheeks of the other cowherd girls. (Gāthā Saptaśatī 114)
The Vindhya mountain sheds its bark as it were, through clouds that have spread toward every quarter of the sky and are clashing against one another with their jagged edges;
meanwhile, the Pulinda hunters, stationed upon the mountain peaks, gaze out with their bows resting [upon their shoulders].
Like the Vindhya mountains being filled by herds of elephants, or like a new cloud;
the Vindhya, its body soiled by the black smoke of forest fires, shines with white clouds like the Slayer of Madhu (Viṣṇu) drenched in milk overflowing from the churning of the ocean of milk.
Even though she was despondent because her kinsmen had been slain, the young thief was gazed upon with affection as one who had escaped;
for who would harbor envy toward virtues? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 118) Today is the very day that the hunter’s wife, intoxicated by her own beauty and youth, [was seen].
She scatters her good fortune upon the streets under the guise of a handful of rice;
the row of parched grain is tossed up by the wind from the courtyard like a banner of her good fortune being raised on a victory pillar. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 119–120)
As she was coming from her father’s house, her husband’s death was carried away by the branches of the *karañja* tree, which were soiled by the rubbing against her cheeks;
he, though thinned by love for his new bride, was protecting the pride of his first wife. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 121)
The hunter carries his bow, though it is difficult to lift because it is smeared with blood.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 122) Even while laughing, Śyāmā, who was giving birth for the first time, said many times to her husband, "I have had enough. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 123)
"O friend, in the world of mortals there is no love at all that is free from separation;

and if there is separation for someone, who can live when separation has occurred? It is like a marvel, like finding a treasure, like sovereignty in heaven, or like drinking nectar. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 124)
For that brief moment, we were both deprived of the sight of her [true] form.
(Gāthā Saptaśatī 125) She is your beloved, you are mine; she is a courtesan, and I am yours, young man.
We say clearly: love, it seems, has many transformations. (Gāthā Saptaśatī 126)
"I am modest, yet his love is so unrestrained;
even my friends are clever—enough! What need is there for a servant? [Thus she speaks] in the forest, which is filled with the humming of bees intoxicated by the spring breeze. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 127)

The cowherd girl’s mind is enchanted by the longing for her lover during their separation; likewise, pride— which is her very wealth— has been so intensely cultivated that even though her beloved has been entreated,
he remains away from home in the very same village.
Even while her husband is still in the sun, the housewife, laughing, takes hold of his feet and washes them even though he does not wish it, as he laughs himself.
"Let my friends call me by her name"—what is the use of saying more? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 130)
"Let there be firm love wherever it may be; do not say anything against it.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 131) "Beauty resides in the eyes, touch in the limbs, what was spoken is in the ears, and the heart is placed within the heart;
so what has Fate separated? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 132)
Having fashioned her beloved out of wish-fulfilling stone upon the bed, she, with eyes closed,
embraced herself with her arms whose bracelets had slipped loose.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 133) Even by one who was humiliated, wandering from house to house all day long for the sake of another's business...
By this long-lived one, whose body is consumed by fire,
that very place where the villain dwells— being nourished with affection and gifts— is, like a lamp, soon soiled by him. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 134–135)
Even though they exist, the wealth and prosperity of a miserly man become utterly fruitless,
like one's own shadow to a traveler scorched by the summer heat. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 136) O left-eyed one, if that beloved of yours comes now that you have shown your affection, then for a long time...
Closing my right eye, I shall gaze upon you without blinking.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 137) Wandering for your sake through a village teeming with dogs, that young woman will one day be devoured by the household dog like a piece of meat. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 138)

Whatever other floral nectar that great honeybee desires to drink is the fault of the sapless flowers, not of the bee. She, whose eyes are like blue lotuses placed in the street, awaits you as you approach. *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 139.
With her two breasts, which are like auspicious jars filled with water, she weeps as long as there is weeping, until her limbs waste away;
that wretched woman sighs as long as her sighs still prevail. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 140–141)
When a couple who have increased their shared happiness and sorrow and whose love has matured over time dies, that indeed is truly living;
the other is dead. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 142) The first cluster of blossoms, accompanied by fresh mango sprouts, will carry away my beloved.
"Do not weep, my daughter; the departure-jar placed at the entrance [foretells] your journey. (GāSa.
143) "That pride, which somehow was sent into my heart by my friends having found an opening—like a secret lover, it has vanished as soon as the beloved was seen. (GāSa. 144)
Being told by her friends, "This is a saffron flower stuck on your breast," the innocent young bride laughs as she brushes away the nail-marks.
O you who are becoming indifferent, these [nail-marks] are as if uprooting your heart.
With half-glances from eyes rolling and unsteady due to the poison of separation,
they neither let out long sighs, nor weep for long, nor become emaciated—
blessed are those women whose lover is beloved by many, but not you.
With the light of her cheeks rolling and trembling as she yawns from the languor of sleep, the glances of the moon-faced one are difficult even for Kāma to endure;
how I have somehow passed through the tossing waves of love with my life remaining but a remnant! (Gāthāsaptaśatī 148)
"O, cease from this! O burnt heart, do not take delight anywhere!
[Gāthāsaptaśatī 149] "At the sight of the lady’s fresh nail-marks, the surface of her breasts—already lofty with heavy youth—becomes as if marked by the lotuses of her own eyes. [Gāthāsaptaśatī 150]

Bow down to him, in whose lap the face of Lakṣmī is seen reflected in his chest-ornament like the orb of the moon or the orb of the sun, never deprived of its luster. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 151) Do not grant happiness to the enemy; appease your beloved, who is fond of being propitiated.
"O daughter, with your heavy pride thus seized, you will waste away like a heap [of grain].
(GāSa 152) In her heart, which is being split by the unbearable saw of separation, the tears—stained with collyrium—appear like a measuring-line. (GāSa 153)
"Difficult to extract, my son; do not act rashly.
Hearts placed here cannot be recovered. Though the bride has finished her meal, she does not know the duration of the sexual rest. *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 154.
She thinks, "There is something else as well that is never lacking. (GāSa.
155) May the loves of courtesans—created by the path of great artifice and removing the thirst for the nectar of the pleasure of gods—bring joy to all the world! (GāSa. 156)
"Since you have not obtained wealth or water, why do you ask me, laughing, 'Why are you so emaciated?
As long as your beloved is fickle-minded, I shall tell you; you have sported with women who cast aside even their own sisters and friends. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 157)
These are the very pleasures for which there is doubt regarding the life of a woman.
(GāSā 158) Her jealous husband does not allow her to pluck the *mahua* flower at night;
yet, being of an exceedingly upright nature, she plucks it herself from her own mother. (GāSā 159)
O traveler, you move slowly with your garment tucked up to your waist;
you think that even the middle of your chest, burdened by heavy breasts, will not break.
As the traveler drinks water for a long time with his eyes upturned and his fingers spread apart, [he does not notice the exhaustion]. *Gāthāsaptaśatī 160*
The beggar likewise thins out his already slender stream [of alms];
he gazes at the circle of the navel, she too [gazes] at his moon-like face;
and both their bodies plunder that skull-like vessel. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 161–162)

Why do you weep so excessively under the pretext of grief,
with such intense longing that your speech falters as it stumbles from the throat, choked by emotion?
Tonight, during the thick darkness of the night, the husband has gone abroad and the house is empty.

Therefore, remain vigilant so that we are not robbed while we sleep. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 336)

"Surely you dwell in my heart as one placed there by her own heart; otherwise, tell me, how could my desires have been understood by her? O fortunate one, when you were departing, she listened with ears pricked by her eyes.
Water has been given by the water-carriers, which is pleasant to behold. (GāSa.

Thus was she addressed by his eyes, which were blossoming with joy, in the midst of the people. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 340)
Even after having consented, with their limbs still perspiring from the exertion,
couples remain in distress with their desires unfulfilled, their curiosity increasing through the mutual exchange of messages. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 341–342)
If he is truly not dear to you, my friend, why does your face become like a lotus blossoming at the touch of the sun’s rays upon his mention by name?
O friend, [he is] the harsh wind to the tree of jealous anger, yet the source of comfort for every limb.
May there be success for the prologue of this drama of the night! (GāSa.
344) O heart, free from suspicion through your own inference, be gracious and desist now; why do you trouble us, following after people who do not understand the ultimate truth? (GāSa. 345)
The lover of the woman who was being praised by her husband for a long time, "She is the moon," became embarrassed as she offered handfuls of flowers to your face;
even while you were visibly wasting away day by day, her limbs [could not bear it]. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 346)
"O child, when questioned, we do not know whom we should say something to. "O teacher of my limbs' emaciation, O instructor of long sighs,

Otherwise, it would truly be impossible to bring to an end the suffering of separation from my beloved— even through the consolation of his death— were it not for the ever-increasing weight of our grief.

O you who are straight as a reed, that excellent woman was today taught by you— through your own transgression— to languish with tears spreading across her face for days on end.

"Do not go, O flower-gatherer; the gods are pleased by the water-offerings with joined palms.

Though she was courageous and self-restrained, when you passed by in front of her elders,

O young man, why have you not been told this over and over again? (GāSa.
371) I now bow down to that very same leader of the Gaṇas who was once bestowed upon my head by young men; O old woman, may you be satisfied! (GāSa. 372)

"Be confident; O fortunate one, we shall endure everything.

380) Today, my friend, at dawn, someone bearing a certain beloved in mind sang a song that serves as a blow to the chest of our hearts pierced by the arrows of Love. (GāSa. 381)
Seeing her breast rising with great effort,
the first wife sighed as she watched the innocent young bride whose cheeks were pressed against it.
[Gāthāsaptaśatī 382] Even for one tormented by intense hunger, the face of his beloved female elephant fills him with satisfaction.
The lotus-stalk morsel, though savory, withered in the hand of him who had departed.
"Be gracious, my dear! Why are you angry, O gentle one? What cause for anger is there in another's word?

Thinking "you will come," she remained awake for the first half of the night as if it were a mere moment;
the remainder passed for her, overcome by anguish, like a year.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 385) Do not fear, do not doubt; this woman is not a female spirit wandering about.
The wives of travelers have their hearts agitated by the thundering of the clouds.
O bee, as much nectar as there is in the lotus amidst its mass of filaments,
if you enjoy that much elsewhere as well, then you shall shine as you wander.

The travelers with unblinking eyes gaze upon the dust raised by the plowman’s oxen—pale as the back of a white elephant—as if it were the early morning twilight, like the splendor of the ocean of milk overflowing its shores.

By her, who was distressed and weeping, even we were made to weep.
"O wretched woman, why do you not now raise up your husband who has fallen at your feet?
This indeed is the end of love, even after it has gone far. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 389–390)

"O Kusumbha, let the young women learn [the ways] through your favor. (GāSa.
392) "How is it that you have not become as broad as the street itself, so that even one who has cast off the shame of elders might touch that handsome man? (GāSa. 393)
Like a peacock in the rainy season drinking a drop of dew clinging to the tip of a blade of grass, the fire of passion drinks the pearl pierced by the needle of love.
The lady’s breast-surface, which overflows from beneath her dark bodice, shines forth.
Like the orb of the moon emerging from within a cloud filled with water;

Blessed are those women who behold their beloved even in a dream;
for without him, sleep does not come at all—who indeed could see a dream?
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 397) [With] ears charming with cheeks adorned by golden earrings...
O friend, by the power of fate, even a pair of palm-leaf fans is discarded. (GāSa.
398) Even for a traveler setting out at midday during the summer, the flow of nectar-water from the moonlight of his beloved’s face, residing in his heart, removes his torment. (GāSa. 399)
Tell me, who would not be angry when entreated in an improper place?
A mother, preoccupied with her own pleasure, even devours her own crying son.
O heart, if you burn, let it burn; if you fester, let it fester; and if you burst, then burst! (Gāthāsaptaśatī 400)
Nevertheless, he remains entirely excluded by me, for his true nature has been exposed. Having seen the tip of his own fang protruding from the corner of his gaping mouth,
even a barren cow grazes in the village pasture at will, even without any purpose.

O Kaṅkelli tree, it is by him alone that there is nothing for you which has not been provided in abundance.
That your sprout is compared to the hand of a beautiful woman— O connoisseur,
expert, playful, and worldly one, you are truly an *aśoka* (shameless), since you bloom at dawn even when struck by the lotus-feet of excellent young women. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 404–405)
Victorious is Hari in the form of Vāmana,

For her whose limbs are refreshed by the bliss of love in the dense embrace of dying,

The village headman’s daughter, growing like a spreading poison-plant, will bring about misfortune.
Bow down to the third foot of Hari, which, though unable to reach the circle of the earth, remains fixed in the sky for a long time,
as if adorned by the leaping-up of the stars.

"In this riverbank, which is being flooded even without any cause," [he says].

They find sleep, they listen to what is told, they do not speak with faltering words—

O young man, having placed the row of heroes given by you upon their ears...

Visible and pleasing to the eye, bringing solace to those who are weary, though he is sought after with folded hands, my beloved—who is like the moon, the abode of all arts—cannot be obtained.
Those clusters on the slopes of the riverbank which were once broken by the weight of clinging bees... [Gāthāsaptaśatī 421]

The bow, straight by nature, hurls the arrow as it falls upon the string;

By her pair of breasts, a bond with the enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) has been established, as if by the binding of the three folds of skin.

Let the abundance of the meritless *kunda* flowers be provided even now. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 426)

The falling even of breasts—which are lofty, closely set, possess the beauty of fresh forest groves, and have accomplished their purpose—is delightful, like that of warriors who have fulfilled their duty;
they are pleasant to the touch, heavy, without gaps between them, marked with auspicious signs, and adorned with ornaments. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 427)
In whose heart do breasts not take root, like the *kavvālāa* plant? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 428) The necklace is cast off from the circles of breasts by young women during the embrace of their lovers;

"O friends,
the nature of the fire of love is such that it is extinguished in the hearts of the dry, but it blazes in those who are moist with emotion.

Even as I fell at her feet, not even the sound was heard from the tree of her affection.

The innocent young bride, unaware, rubs for a moment, washes for a moment,

(Gāthāsaptaśatī 433) When the rainy season has passed, like youth with its swelling breasts.

In the sky, Time is weaving a *valākāvatī* cloth, as if on a loom. (GāSa 435)

O heart, having then accepted the command of your lover for a full day, [why do you now grieve? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 436).
Why have you begun this act that destroys trust and causes distress?
She tells this even to one who does not know it; her bracelets have been broken by him, for she is too simple-minded, or else her beloved is a laughingstock to her. (GāSa. 437–438)
Ah! At the base of her cheek, which is filled with the excellence of her youthful beauty, her loveliness is drunk by the shoulder of her ear as if with a downward-turned face—

Addressing him thus, she arrived at the very courtyard of his house.

wipe away [the pollen] even before you have attained the full expansion of the bud. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 443–444)
O shameless one, that village mud which I trampled in the autumn rains for your sake— I still look upon it today with indifference, O you who have no sense of shame!
It shines there, with hair falling away, earrings dangling, and necklaces and garlands swaying.
O young man, you are like a Vidyādhara who has arrived prematurely;

At the hour of twilight, bow to the Lord of the Dawn, who holds his cupped hands filled with water, with his left arm slightly extended,

Even among the breasts, the gaze turns toward the one who is dearer.

Turn away from those other words that flow forth from my heart;

"Is it that one's name is stolen while alive, and having stolen it, it is given back to me?

Victorious is the third eye of Rudra, which was transformed into a mountain!

A young woman binds a white cloth around her hips like a merchant’s shop-sign.

This moon-bright night, like a doe-eyed gazelle, is fading away.

Either the beloved of Gaurī’s heart, or King Śālavāhana.

You have been struck by our hands as we ran forward with trembling fingers.

Her thirst for knowledge grows dense with every moment; horripilation arises, yet it does not manifest in the heart.
Nothing else remains—only the vital breaths, intensified by the pursuit of modesty.
For those who do not understand the essence of the sounds of lutes and flutes, nor of those mature women, that alone is their punishment.
When the Goddess Śrī saw Brahmā situated upon the lotus of his navel during the reverse sexual union, [she was filled with wonder].
The deer quickly covers his right eye with his hand, overcome by passion.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 816) Great beings, whose distress is produced by the casting of glances from the eyes of graceful women, perish;
they become unable to endure the agitation of their minds. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 817)
Laugh in such a way that you do not become ridiculous; speak in such a way that it is pleasing to others; live in such a way that you attain fame; die in such a way that you are not reborn.
O bee, enter the winter [of the season] with the flowers of the palace; for now, do not die.
If you live, you shall behold the prosperity of spring once again.
(Gāthā Saṃgraha 819) In every place there is a dwelling for donkeys and buffaloes, for rams and bulls, and for noble elephants;
alas, [this is] either a great forest or a great king! (Gāthā Saṃgraha 820)
"Father, I am not the field; let the rice be eaten by the flocks of parrots!
Even though they know it, travelers ask for the way again and again. [Thus speaks] the daughter-in-law before her elders when her son-in-law arrives unexpectedly. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 821)

O beautiful one, who has not been subdued by these eyes of yours— white on the outside, dark in the middle, and throbbing with joy as they fall [upon him]— which are like malicious informants clinging to the ears? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 822–823)
"Come, look at this with astonished hearts, friends!
She gazes at her cheek in the mirror, and at the mirror on the surface of her cheek.
"When was she born? When indeed was she taught this artifice, O mother? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 824)
Know that women know everything that is to be known. (GāSa.

825) O daughter, with breasts grey from being rubbed every moment, with eyes tawny like honey-liquor, and adorned with earrings of *kuvalaya* flowers and mango-blossom clusters—you have decorated the village. (GāSa. 826)
When the beloved’s single lip is found by the path, kissed with forceful passion, and brought to oneself, the various cravings for its flavors become manifold.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 827) [With eyes wide open and perspiration flowing down the cheeks...]
Even without speaking, her accomplishment of the task was expressed by her face. (GāSa.
828) Where there is no wakefulness [of jealousy], where there is no distress from envy, where there is no pride, and where there is no affectionate deceit—there love does not exist. (GāSa. 829)
"O proud one, why do you paint my name on your pair of breasts, saying it was written by my great lover?
If he were truly her lover, there would not even be a tremor.
Thus [she says] to me, an unfortunate woman, as it fell upon my ear and indeed fell into my heart. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 830)
Did you not endure my words, "She is my sister," regarding your departure?

(GāSā 831) Even for a traveler on the road who has set out with another, his steps falter on the first day of the journey as if weighed down by the heavy burden of his wife held in his heart. (GāSā 832)
Not even a message was written by the traveler in his letter; for where could there be news of the household on a leaf already filled with the incessantly written syllables of his wife’s family name?
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 833) [She is] one whose perspiration has doubled as she yearns for the touch of her husband’s limbs, which have arrived through her longing.
Even though winter has passed, it was not noticed by the woman whose husband is away.
May she obtain the pleasures of an embrace with her limbs overflowing with the thrill of horripilation from having found her beloved in a dream; do not wake her.
The series of sighs of the wife of the traveler, who was unable to endure the long separation from her beloved, extinguishes the lamp as she rises—
those sighs which were drunk in by her on the first day of the journey due to her auspicious impressions. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 836)

The water of her tears does not remain [in her eyes] while she weeps in separation; rather, her longing and lack of desire cause her entire retinue to weep, as she gazes with eyes swollen and filled with tears. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 837–838)
Just as the end of day, rendered fragrant by breezes heavy with the scent of fresh sirīsa flowers,

does not burn so intensely for the wife of the traveler— even at midday— so too [is the heat of separation] when she is sustained by clever friends with stories of her long-absent beloved for the sake of enduring their separation. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 839)
Moreover, the various offenses of the young wife are recounted in succession. (GāSa.

840) When a woman whose husband is away from home writes the syllables of her beloved’s name in a letter, the crow wipes them away with its beak, which has become moistened by the traces of the ink used for writing. (GāSa. 841)
"Let her remain with eyes closed; do not, do not ward her off from the hope of her beloved!
What would she see even with eyes opened without him?
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 842) Long, hot sighs, restless longing, and a song choked with weeping.
In the separation from loved ones, this alone is the solace for those who cherish life.
(Gāthāśataka 843) O Fate, if you are pleased with me, do not grant me a human birth;
if there must be a birth, let there be no love; if there must be love, let it not be for a person difficult to find. (Gāthāśataka 844)
The world says that nights are indeed short in the summer;
but as for me, separated from my beloved, I do not know why they grow longer.
One day becomes two, and the nights become long.
In this world, two things alone increase without precedent: the longing for life and the longing for death.
O you who desire long life, do not seek separation from those unstable objects of pleasure, by which the days of youth are made to pass away. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 846–847)
While I weep, she counts the days until our meeting;
like me in the separation from her beloved, O friend, the affection of my companion is indeed unprecedented. [This is] through the embrace of the neck and the hospitable service of my companion.
When her husband returned, the face of the young wife became calm.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 849) O moon-faced one, O lotus-armed one, O lotus-eyed one, even the moon, the lotus-stalks, and the blue lotuses torment you in your separation. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 850)
O beloved, you are under the control of your elders; what can I say to you, unfortunate as I am?
Today you are departing on a journey—go! You yourself know what must be done.
O you with broad hips and full breasts, the expanse of the earth is vast. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 851)
"O fair one, you may find broad-eyed young women; do not grieve.
Seeing you whose passion has faded even without cause, that poor girl is distressed by the suspicion of her own faults in her heart. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 852–853)
The messenger has not come; the moon has risen; the night too passes away.
Everything everywhere is utterly disordered—what can we say? The messenger went and delays; "Will he come to my side, or will he not?"—[I wonder]. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 854)
The heart of her who stands suspended between life and death is like a swing. (GāSa.
855) Look! As the female messenger, overflowing with playful jests, says "He has not come," a thrill of joy spreads across the sides of her cheeks. (GāSa. 856)
"Where indeed did he go? How was he seen? What was said?
Or what was replied by him?"—thus she speaks repeatedly, unable to finish, her mind anxiously looking for signs on the face of the female messenger. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 857)
Her heart trembles with a longing for union that is both tender and playful;
those words she sent to you, which I did not perceive, were spoken with syllables faltering and uneven due to her exceedingly hot sighs. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 858–859)
"O friend, you have endured suffering moment by moment for my sake;
you have indeed performed what was required by our mutual affection and sincerity.
For you yourself always say: 'Whatever is your business, that alone is my business.'"
O you who speak the truth, today you have reached the further shore of that [matter].
(GāSā 861) That which was done by the farmer’s wife, who had fainted from the blow of the fresh ploughshare, is what even today young women strive to learn in every house. (GāSā 862)
"O Dhanya! O Haliddaja!
You are truly fortunate, for even as your husband gazes upon you, flowers fall from the slopes of the full breasts of the daughter of the plowman.
"It is indeed true that the Lord of the Gods (Indra) is made of wood, since [he was unable to protect] the daughter of the plowman..."
With hands as tender as lotus petals, she has not even been touched by him.
Thus, unfortunate and with her desires unfulfilled, I shall perish;
yet even public rumor regarding me and that son of a farmer has not arisen.
In the homes of the fortunate, wives possess modesty, full maturity, and beauty; they are free from thirst for the prosperity of others and are devoid of delusion.
Their laughter is innocent and free from artifice, and their movements possess the natural grace of those separated from lovers.
In the home of the fortunate, the speech of their wives is naturally straightforward;
yet when the husband describes the beauty of his neighbor’s beautiful wife, the housewife utters a grunt heavy with jealousy and envy. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 867–868)

The manifestations of pride are carried away by no one, nor are they revealed; they lament within the heart of the woman who guards her family honor—more empty than a void, yet nourished by the compassion of her enemies. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 869)
Her eyes alleviate the longing of separation by acting as guardians of the family lineage.

(GāSā 870) Behold, for the virtuous wife, the charms and playful graces of youth depart when her husband is away on a journey, and they return as if entering the home when her beloved returns. (GāSā 871)
"Right before my eyes, my husband was kissed with impetuosity by the unchaste woman;
'your mouth smells of wine,' she says, weeping.
Thus did the unchaste woman weep at her husband's death, her throat choked with tears.
Just as the heart of a husband is filled with apprehension when he fears his wife might die,
so too do the limbs of the young bride shiver as she hears the clamor of birds flying up from the thicket of reeds while she is occupied with her household chores.
My mother-in-law, whose mind is never weary, urges me on with the entirety of the household burden;
even for a mere moment at twilight, there is no rest at all.
At every spot, at every turn, she drags me along with her entire household and its attendants.
“You have not come to our village, brother-in-law, nor have you seen the Muralā river.
“O young man, why do you rob me of my hips with your honeyed words?
Even if I were to tell the truth, to whom could I speak in this forest where the village is far away and I am all alone?”
O religious man, ruined by the letter of the time, you are like a worm in a neem tree;
if the residence in hell for both of us is equal, then let it be so.
O traveler, there is no lodging here in this village of stony ground. *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 878.
"O you with swelling breasts, if you wish to dwell [here], then dwell!
O friend, seeing you with your trembling eyes and ill-omened marks, the wall, fearing contact with the water, has split itself apart as if its own body were too heavy. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 879–880)
"Friend, having taken this large water-jar, I have returned quickly;
now, unable to endure the equal flow of tears and breaths, I shall rest for a moment.
People laugh at my following him in death, yet I cannot even weep as I desire. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 881)
"What shall I do here now that my lover, the thief, has departed? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 882) "Do not speak such crooked words, my daughter, in front of these rogues;
for even their laughter understands what has been said in their hearts. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 883)
"Where can there be crooked speech? Where can there be side-long glances? One cannot even breathe freely in a village surrounded by rogues.
"Even there, my dear child, there are friends; do not weep where you have been given away."
Even there is the charm of dense thickets; even there flows the river Godāvarī.
Whose anger would not arise upon seeing his beloved’s bitten lower lip?
O you who are perverse in warding off the bee that seeks the lotus, endure this now!
"Even flattened rice is eaten when there are no other grains; daughter, what fault is there in this?

One may take pleasure even with one's own husband in a village that is free from strangers. "Let some other person speak whatever they wish; one who has not known the pleasure of a stranger's touch speaks thus. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 887)
"Even with our own husbands, we take pleasure only in thinking of them as strangers. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 888) "Mother, you said today there were no household provisions;
so tell me, what should be done? The day does not stand still like this. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 889)
Who is able to describe the playful charm of intense passion, nourished by her own desire and delight in seeing him, as it is sported by a highly skilled courtesan?
Even in ordinary beautiful women, it is indeed lack of restraint that brings about such amorous grace.
Even the smoke of burning fragrant wood is indeed sweet.
Alas, the course of time! That youth, too, who was so fond of elegant poetry, now utters the sound "parāsara" (a cry of distress); we, for our part, shall go to our own husband.
Bow down to the feet of Māna, O friend! What is the use of other gods?
By his grace alone, a lover rolls at one's side. [He grants] the festival of falling at one's feet without the need for conciliation, and the blissful joy of impetuous kisses.
These and other such things cause pride to bear fruit as if it were helpless.
O little doll, if you have need of much happiness from conciliation, then weep for a moment while that [man] is still well-disposed; do not maintain your pride.
An order is given by one who does not speak; it is seen that he turns his back as she departs, and he sighs, "O daughter, this pride of yours is indeed unprecedented!
When the friends say, "We shall do exactly that," she replies, "Yes, I will certainly do it."
If my fortitude could have been restrained when he approached me, [it would have failed];
for though rebuked by my glance, he draws near; though struck, he clings to me; though beaten, the shameless one kisses me by force—how indeed can I be angry? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 897–898)
"O friends, how can I possibly maintain jealous anger toward my beloved, when even the nights, their hands smeared with camphor powder, display their pride before him?
What do you say to me, friends? 'Maintain your anger! But what is the use of anger? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 899)
When he has been excluded from all social circles, there is no need for me to maintain pride even toward him.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 900) "Friends, when the beloved is not seen, tell me, whose pride could possibly be maintained?
But if pride is maintained even when he is seen, then how can he be considered a beloved? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 901)
I know my transgression; I know she speaks all those words falsely.
But when she seeks to appease me, I know myself as one who has committed a transgression.
When he is not seen, we shall bear thousands of offenses within our hearts.
But regarding what has been seen, we do not remember even a single thing of our dear friend. (GāSa.
903) Speak, speak! Whatever seems right to you, we shall endure it; for both my lack of fortitude and my life, O beloved, cannot coexist. (GāSa. 904)
"O handsome one, say, say this very name of mine! Why do you appear so distracted?
It seems as though it does not belong to you; why then should it belong to me? "O handsome one, sleep for a moment; you shall be called by whatever name pleases you."
"Today they do not look at you, their eyes heavy with sleep. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 906) "Do not trouble her greatly, my son, with false names;
she herself knows well enough our joking and playful speech. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 907)

"O fierce one, do you not see that if he calls out under another name, it is because he wishes to see your face dancing with jealousy? O simple girl, you are being provoked by errors of name; do not weep. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 908)
Or why else would she not look with eyes so large? (GāSa.
909) One cannot find comfort in sleep; alas, through the moment-by-moment falling at the feet of love—which is crooked, treacherous, and like a bedstead difficult to construct—(GāSa. 910)
On the single bed, the fair-faced woman, having become averse due to the heavy bond of pride during a quarrel in her sleep, has now become face-to-face.
"Let your pride increase, you who speak such defiant words!"—GāSa. 911.
"Truth, sleep does not come without you; grant me an opportunity.
The tree of anger, its offenses made manifest through the lover's artful speech, suddenly sprouts again upon her eyes and cheeks. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 912–913)
Proud women, when being entreated, tear their very hearts out;
their faces are overwhelmed by a flood of tears born from the weight of resentment they have long cherished.
They do not weep so much even from the pain of the momentary anger that was quickly appeased.

Just as young women, when their beloved is seen and they are being entreated, [strike him]; so too, the proud woman, desiring with her heart a kick from her foot that had been raised in anger, did not strike her lover with her head, but wept profusely with tears. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 915–916)
Even though she did not speak while giving her dear friend the necklace bestowed by her beloved without having informed her, the resentment of that proud woman was already expressed.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 917) He will go to her house; he will find an opportunity; he will come into her presence.
She will say what ought to be said; what indeed will she receive in reply?
O cruel one, with your face shrouded in darkness, that poor woman is made to waste away day by day like the crescent of the moon during the thick of the night.
O lotus-eyed one, today my beloved has done me a kindness by not frowning— a gesture that would have bestowed a fresh beauty upon your face—
and by not speaking harshly or pressing her lip against mine. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 920)
"She was served by him but did not weep; from this too, we recognize her pride. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 921) "You say nothing at all, yet you do exactly as you are told;
though your heart is quickly overcome with anger, your very modesty proclaims it. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 922)
Though questioned, you do not speak; when kissed by force, you snatch away your face.
O lotus-eyed one, when I am intent on playfulness, you distress my heart.
O fair-limbed one, with a face supported by your full breasts, listen to my words!
"O beloved, it is not fitting to maintain pride during this transient youth. (GāSa.
924) "O you with tremulous eyes, moon-like face, breasts like those of an elephant, and a slender waist—how indeed can one maintain pride when the long winter nights do not end? (GāSa. 925)
"Though you are happy, beautiful, young, and proud, O daughter, why do you grieve like a sandalwood staff scorched by fire?
Even before your rival, you were told by him, 'Be gracious'. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 926)
O proud woman, what other fruit is there for maintaining pride? (GāSa.

927) You pull back my hand as it moves toward your waistband; you turn your face away and refuse to release your arm; you hold back your heavy sighs—O proud one, your knowledge of pride is great indeed! (GāSa. 928)
"Even without any business, you have displayed such grandiosity; with every limb bristling with horripilation, longing for the joy of a tight embrace—you have been recognized, daughter!
"Ha! Friend, what indeed have I not seen while I am still clinging to life?"
"He entreats me, he is my beloved, and I too am entreated by him"—such are our jests.
As long as there is no room for longing, so long is there happiness and delight;
but when love is directed toward a man with many favorites, who is the very seat of suffering, there is no such opportunity.
He cannot be restrained by those who cherish their honor; some offender, having committed an undesirable act, must be led away like one brought for counsel.
She bears the weight of her anger, which was seized by her lover and then consumed by the fire of Hara’s lips.
Like a mirror made of crystal, the face of the young woman reflects the wine flowing from her mouth;
yet when her lover, impetuous in his embrace, presses close, her pride quickly slips away from her heart as if terrified of being squeezed out. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 933–934)
O friend, that mountain of pride which I had fashioned— high, firm,
and vast— has not withstood the blow of the thunderbolt of my lover’s glance.
O friend, having created an opening for my pride through my own steadfastness...

"By him, thinking 'suddenly' when my eyes were distressed by the sight of my beloved, [the garment] was cast off. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 936) O dark-limbed one, with your body revealed by your nails and your eyes rolling in sleep, you do not distress my heart as much as you do when your lips are silent. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 937)
O you who act as if you were right before my eyes, if you kiss these cheeks of mine,
then why do you especially thirst for my dear friend? At that time,
you did not turn your gaze away from my cheek.
Now it is indeed the same I, those same cheeks, yet that gaze is not the same.
O handsome one, such has become the end of those appreciations of virtue, of those longings, of that love, and of those conversations. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 939–940)
O fortunate one, though you are appeasing me as if I were angry even when I am not, I grieve for the loss of those days; it is not that I am truly angry.
Yes, O beloved, there is no fault of yours here; the fault lies with my eyes.
I have been pierced in my heart by those fickle arrows that are unbearable to the mind.
O handsome one, what fault of yours is there? Alas, my heart! You look at me with cruel eyes and speak without blinking; you do not speak with humility behind my back. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 942–943)
Let the sighs and weeping belong to her alone;

let them not be known even to you, whose nature is so gentle, while following a person like me who is born of noble lineage. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 944) Following a person like me who is born of noble lineage...
But in her heart she thought again: "Only one born of a noble family can achieve happiness.
"O shameless one, come here! Go and appease that very woman by whom this tilaka was fashioned with the juice of lac from her big toe. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 945–946)
She dwells in your heart; she alone remains in your eyes; and she is in your dreams.
O handsome one, where is there any opportunity for wretches like us? My thirst for your affection—how could we possibly know how that might be?

Therefore, handsome one, you yourself must instruct me so that I may become dear to you. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 948) In those who wear soiled garments, whose hands are calloused from labor, and whose cheeks are pale with toil—even for these women of the flower-sellers, Kāma dwells within their limbs as if he were a warrior. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 949)
"I am a flower-seller, young man; do not speak thus. You will have but a short life.
Let her die this very day; what is the use of wasting time? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 950) "O merchant, where are there elephant tusks for us? We have only tiger-claws."
Meanwhile, the daughter-in-law wanders about the house with her face disheveled by bees.
The female swans seize the hearts of their beloved mates with their broad beaks,
as if those hearts were the hollows of the arrows of the Flower-Wielder (Kāma).
The beauty of the swans is surpassed by the lotuses, and that of the lotuses by the swans;
indeed, these two alone hold themselves in high esteem.
As the breasts of the young maiden grow day by day, they become increasingly radiant.

In every way, like a wind that has found its way, love enters my heart. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 954) Your hair has turned white, your skin is withered from association with unchaste women, and your mind is ruined; yet your good fortune acts as a messenger to the Godāvarī river. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 955)
"Insomnia, physical weakness, anxiety, lethargy, and sighing—
alas, O friend, these afflict you too on account of me, an unfortunate woman! (Gāthāsaptaśatī 956) "O traveler, eager to see your own wife, go by another path!"

In this village, the housewife’s daughter-in-law is difficult to find, and the husband is away. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 957) “O ox, as much as has been obtained by another, that is not enough for you; have patience!
Now the master’s field is being guarded. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 958)
"Pick the fallen flowers; do not shake the *sephālikā* tree, daughter-in-law of the farmer!
This sound of the plowman's staff, harsh at its conclusion, has been heard by your father-in-law.
Thus she speaks, entering the door of the house with her face turned back as she gazes upon the path.
"Alas! Leaving the jar behind, you weep, 'It is lost! O friend, why do you lament?
"Do not block the path; go away, young man! We have lost all our modesty; you tread upon us as if upon an empty house that cannot look back."
"It is heard that your husband will arrive this very day at the end of a watch;
why then do you remain thus? O friend, prepare what must be done.
"O dear sister-in-law, you who have arrived for a moment, why have you struck me, O handsome one?"
Let the poor woman be entreated in the house of the *phalinī* creeper at the edge of the dwelling where she weeps;
let her be petitioned by the young trees on the ground, bowed down by the weight of their flowers,
and by the *madhuka* bees in the vast thickets of the Godāvarī forest.
In every house where a paramour has been introduced by the mistress, the mistress stands nearby and speaks with the paramour; afterwards, both the mistress and the householder [are caught].
On one side the beloved weeps, on the other side the roar of the battle-drum.
The warrior’s heart wavers between affection and the passion for battle.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 966) O wicked one, unaware that she was feigning anger during a playful jest, the wife has truly burst into tears; desist from your mockery! (Gāthāsaptaśatī 967)
Therefore, turn back out of favor; you who have dispelled the mass of darkness with the moonlight of your face, you cause an obstacle for the female attendants and even bring laughter to others.
Your lightness is one thing, and your manner of walking is quite another.
"O Sāmā, you are indeed the very ornament of the commoners' protector; you do not merely exist.
"O daughter, he is the foremost of rogues, possessing dull hair and abundant wealth"—when this was said, Naaṅgī’s eyes blossomed wide with joy. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 969–970)
"By the rays of the nails of your hands, which are like lotus stalks, you have bestowed a red silk cloth upon my eyes as a favor;
however, out of anger, these [eyes] have not been stepped upon.
"Come, come here first, O beautiful one! Lend me your ear and listen to what must be said."

"O slender-waisted one, because of your face, the moon is compared by people [to it]. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 972) "With breasts of such size, with eyes of such size, in such a state, in just so many days. (Gāthāsaptaśatī 973)
Salutations to the horripilation of Kṛṣṇa, who remembered Pañcajanya while his lips were pressed against the mouth of the breast of Yaśodā, which was held by his hand.
What is the way of destiny so perverse? What is difficult to obtain if people are appreciative of virtue?
What is happiness? A good wife. What is suffering? That the world is wicked. (GāSa.
975) The wealth of the miserly, the crest-jewels of serpents, the manes of lions, and the breasts of noble women—where do these things perish, if not for those who are dead? (GāSa. 976)
Having twisted her hair by the roots, he seized Jayasirī in battle, just as the distressed women were firmly established in his throat by the caves.
Though the conduct of the wicked appears cruel, such is the case even for the steadfast.
Resolutions that are firmly rooted in the heart and well-considered do not indeed fail. (GāSā.
978) That which is impossible to abandon even in thought because of its quality of beauty—only its fault has been accepted by those who have looked back [at it]. (GāSā. 979)

In whose inner apartments, even as he wields the sword-blade in his hand, the enemy army suddenly turns its back, though it had previously faced him with passion—people say that the saying "the wound belongs to him who inflicts it" is false. *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 980. The wound belongs to him alone; people call that a lie.
The pain from a toothache in the cheek belongs to the wife, while that of the co-wives is [the pain of] jealousy.
(Gāthāsaptaśatī 981) Just as it is deep, just as it is filled with jewels, and just as it has a stainless luster, why was this ocean not made by Fate to be full of salt? (Gāthāsaptaśatī 982)
